source.title: A Latent Variable Framework for Scaling Laws in Large Language Models
source.authors: Pei-Yao Cai; Cheng-Yu Cui; F. Polo; Seamus Somerstep; Leshem Choshen; Mikhail Yurochkin; Moulinath Banerjee; Yue-Kai Sun; Ke-An-Ming Tan; Gong-Jun Xu

record.file_problem: Full paper and supplementary material are present. No material truncation or garbling that prevents reading the relevant results.
record.tranche_reason: Extends scaling analysis to leaderboard benchmark performance and skill-specific compute allocation, rather than testing the original pretraining-loss scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The study uses leaderboard benchmark scores, not held-out pretraining cross-entropy loss. It reports held-out benchmark prediction results relevant to V6. Table 2 reports compute-optimal allocations for skill performance, not loss minimization; these are recorded under fits_no_version rather than treated as tests of V3. Classical loss laws and results attributed to cited works are background, not rows.
record.test_reason: The study fits a scaling model of downstream leaderboard scores on log parameters and log tokens, using observational data from about 285 open LLMs, and predicts held-out larger models. It bears on V6 in a new setting: observational, multi-family, benchmark accuracy rather than loss. It does not measure pretraining loss, so V1–V5 and V7 are untested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that a few interpretable latent skills (math, instruction following, common sense, logical reasoning) explain performance across 12 benchmarks. These skills grow predictably with model size and training tokens, but at skill-specific rates. Family-specific latent abilities are needed, so a single aggregate law is inadequate. The model gives held-out prediction intervals that nearly always contain observed scores, and implies skill-dependent compute-optimal allocations.
record.recipe_differences: The study develops a likelihood-based latent-variable model for benchmark scores, with family-level latent abilities and benchmark-specific loadings; it does not reproduce the original pretraining-loss fitting procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: Skill-specific optimal allocations differ by skill. The authors report that alternative anchor-benchmark choices leave overall loading patterns similar and do not affect inference for β. Prediction interval widths vary by benchmark.

fits_no_version.finding: The fitted latent-skill model implies skill-specific compute-optimal splits under a fixed FLOPs budget. MATH optima are token-heavy; HellaSwag and BBH optima are parameter-heavy. Many optima sit at imposed data-range bounds or at the 180B/15T caps.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Compute-optimal parameter/token allocation for downstream skill scores differs by skill, unlike a single loss-based optimum.

record.problems: The empirical analysis uses observational leaderboard data; the paper notes possible bias if missingness depends on unobserved benchmark-specific outcomes. Prediction results are reported qualitatively in the main text without a numerical overall interval-coverage rate, and some test ground-truth scores were unavailable. The Table 4 MAE comparison is omitted from rows because the provided flattened table layout does not reliably assign its values to methods and benchmarks.
record.rows_left_out: Table 4 predictive MAE comparisons omitted because the provided flattened layout does not reliably associate all method values with benchmark columns. No Table 2 allocations omitted.

untested.parts: No held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute.
No loss-law extrapolation from small to large training runs.
No loss-minimising allocation. Table 2 optimises downstream skill scores within bounded data ranges.
No controlled architecture or shape comparison at fixed parameters.
No other modalities, repeated-data or transfer scaling. Fine-tuned models are treated as separate families, not as a fine-tuning scaling law.
No test of how loss exponents or the loss-optimal split depend on fitting choices. Anchor-choice robustness concerns the latent model's loadings, not scaling-law exponents.

missing.what: Covariate effects of log(size) and log(tokens) on each latent skill, with SEs. All size and token effects are positive and significant, e.g. MATH log(t) 0.774 (0.086), HellaSwag log(s) 0.840 (0.064), IFEval log(s) 0.190 (0.055). Interaction terms are mostly non-significant. This is direct evidence that downstream skills improve with scale.

Held-out-family MAE by scaling law. The 'All' column appears to be listed bottom-up in the flattened text; reading it that way gives FLOPs 0.142, Size/Tokens/Interaction 0.110, Family/FLOPs 0.048, Family/Size/Tokens/Interaction 0.061, Ours d=4 0.071, Sloth d=3 0.059. This ordering matches the text's statement that the method slightly underperforms Family/FLOPs. The baseline laws' errors bear on V6 even though the method comparison itself is not a claim row.
Per-family scaling with model size at fixed token count for LLaMA-3-Instruct and Qwen-2-Instruct, with prediction intervals.

record.verdict_notes: The study's own outcome is benchmark accuracy modelled through a Beta/IRT latent model, not loss. Prediction tests are within-family size extrapolation (Section 4.4) and held-out-family prediction (Appendix E.4). Data are observational with v1/v2 missingness that the authors admit could bias results. The study is not an original source. Table 2 allocations are model outputs constrained by data-range bounds, so they should not be read as evidence about a power-law compute-optimal split.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not measure held-out pretraining loss against parameter count, tokens, or compute.
The study does not fit pretraining-loss laws on small training runs and test extrapolation to substantially larger runs.
Table 2 optimizes downstream latent-skill performance, not pretraining loss; it does not test whether loss-minimizing parameter and token counts follow the stated powers of compute.
No controlled comparison of architectures at fixed parameter count.
No tests of other modalities, repeated data, or fine-tuning/transfer power laws of the stated form.
Tests prediction of a limited set of held-out leaderboard benchmark scores from the proposed model; it does not establish prediction via pretraining loss or across downstream tasks generally.
Alternative anchor choices are examined, but the paper does not test how pretraining-loss exponents or loss-optimal allocations vary with fitting choices, nor whether loss curves bend.

rows.subject: held-out test LLMs (aggregate)
rows.size_stated: Test set includes Qwen-2-72B, Yi-1.5-34B, Yi-1.5-34B-chat, Meta-llama-3-70B, Meta-llama-3-70B-instruct, Olmo-7B, Smollm1.7b, Smollm-1.7b-instruct, Gemma-2-9b, and Gemma-2-9b-it; the Figure 4 caption says eleven test LLMs.
rows.operation_detail: Constructed 95% prediction intervals for held-out benchmark scores using the fitted scaling model.

conditions.value: held-out models with smaller variants represented in training; test-family-related models of the same size omitted
12 Open LLM Leaderboard benchmarks; some ground-truth scores unavailable

rows.measure: Containment of observed benchmark scores by 95% prediction intervals
rows.value: Nearly all intervals contain the observed scores
rows.note: The outcome is reported for the test set in aggregate, not as a numerical coverage rate. The text lists ten model names, while the figure caption says eleven.
rows.check: State is right. The test models are larger members of families whose smaller variants were in training (footnote 3), so this is within-family extrapolation in size. There is no numeric coverage rate. Appendix E.3 says most interval width comes from intrinsic response noise, which makes containment a weaker test. Text lists 10 test models; the Figure 4 caption says eleven.

rows.subject: held-out test LLMs (aggregate)
rows.size_stated: Test set includes Qwen-2-72B, Yi-1.5-34B, Yi-1.5-34B-chat, Meta-llama-3-70B, Meta-llama-3-70B-instruct, Olmo-7B, Smollm1.7b, Smollm-1.7b-instruct, Gemma-2-9b, and Gemma-2-9b-it; the Figure 4 caption says eleven test LLMs.
rows.operation_detail: Examined benchmark-specific prediction intervals and scaling behavior.
rows.measure: Benchmark performance scaling and prediction-interval width
rows.value: Intervals are wider for GPQA and MuSR; performance on these benchmarks does not scale cleanly with parameter count
rows.note: The text identifies these benchmarks as exceptions; it gives no numerical interval widths or coverage by benchmark.
rows.check: State is right. The authors say GPQA and MuSR performance does not scale cleanly with parameter count and their intervals are wider. No numbers are given.

rows.subject: proposed scaling model (skill-specific optimum)
rows.operation_detail: Optimized skill performance subject to a fixed FLOPs budget; reported the selected parameter and token allocation.
rows.measure: Optimal allocation (parameters in B; training tokens in T)
rows.note: Downstream skill optimum, not a pretraining-loss optimum.
rows.check: These are model-derived allocations that maximise a latent skill score, not loss. Many sit at imposed bounds: the 180B / 15T caps, and MATH stays at 0.07B, the lower data-range bound, for the first four budgets. They are outputs of the study's own optimisation, not measured effects, so 'observed' states are not meaningful. Keep them under fits_no_version only.
